utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Good morning to you, Ms. Lindsay, again. Welcome back to the courtroom. Yesterday I made a mistake. I said the Prosecution indicated that they need ten hours, but in fact they indicated eight hours, as the Defence did. And just to let you know, you have used six hours and 17 minutes for examination-in-chief. You should hurry up, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome back to the courtroom. Again, I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning your testimony two days ago still applies. Mr. Thayer has more questions for you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning again, to you and Your Honours. Good morning to the Defence. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 223, please. When we left off yesterday we were looking at the report that was issued on the 4th of July, 1995, and I'm speaking of the combat readiness analysis report for the first half of 1995. To save a little bit of time, I'm going to skip over a couple of sections of this report. And I would just ask you, do you recall whether there's an entry in the report that lists the sniper training that a number of Bratunac Brigade soldiers underwent?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat report that I see in front of me, or its contents, there is an portion that refers to sniper training, and I believe that that is part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And just for the record that's at page 7 of the English, page 13 of the B/C/S, if anybody wants to look at that in the future. If we could go to page 17 of the English. And that will be page 31 of the B/C/S. Actually, make that page 16, the previous page, and page 29 of the B/C/S. We can see here a section that is entitled: Intelligence security support. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what role you played, if any, in putting together this portion of the combat readiness analysis report?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday, and I think the day before as well, when I spoke about this document, the analysis of combat readiness, that was prepared by the Bratunac Brigade command and, of course, signed by the commander Blagojevic, each of the officers, or, rather, each assistant commander and myself, as the chief of the organ, were obliged to provide information - in my particular case that is security and intelligence - hat is to say, to give our contribution to this report, and that is what I did. I wrote my report, and after I had drafted my proposal and after the commander and the other officers and I, myself, discussed this at a meeting, these contributions were accepted by the commander, including my contribution on security and intelligence, and all the tasks that I was obliged to carry out within my remit. So everything that you see here is something that I put on paper. It was accepted by the commander, and it became an integral part of this analysis on combat readiness. And one of the elements of combat readiness is intelligence and security support of unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in English. And we'll need to go two pages in the B/C/S, to page 31 in the B/C/S, please. This is the next page under the heading of intelligence security support, sir. Do you see the portion that begins: "During 1995 international organisations and their representatives have passed through and stayed temporarily in the brigade's area of responsibility"? Do you see that paragraph, sir? I think it's the third paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I -- I see this paragraph, and I can see what it speaks about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You report that these international organisations and their representatives, when they stayed, their activities were monitored and every significant event was promptly reported to the Drina Corps and the VRS Main Staff. And you refer here to superior organs. What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular instance, but in other instances of reporting as well, I was referring to superior organs that I had communication line with in the corps command or in the Main Staff. So if I say here that I reported to superior officers, I was referring to the intelligence and security department of the Drina Corps, and their counterpart at the level of the Main Staff. It was both my duty and the right to report to my superiors at the Drina Corps and in the Main Staff when it comes to the professional line of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in the next paragraph you report that: "In the brigade's area of responsibility, a check-point was established for the control of all international organisations entering and leaving the enclave of Srebrenica. This check-point functions in accordance with the orders of the VRS ... Main Staff and instructions and orders of the brigade commander." Can you tell the Trial Chamber approximately when this check-point was set up?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I really cannot give you an exact date. I cannot recall at the moment, and I wouldn't like to speculate. But it may have been that it took place immediately, or for a certain period of time we had check-points elsewhere but we had problems, and then we decided to set up a check-point on the Yellow Bridge. But I really don't know. However, this refers to what you read, and I can say that this check-point was set up based on an order from the Main Staff and the instructions issued later by the brigade command. However, when that happened exactly, I really cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 223.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 223 shall be assigned Exhibit P2167. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to turn your attention now to the Krivaja '95 operations and the events following the fall of the enclave. What I'd like to do because our time is limited, is rather than take you through a detailed day-by-day chronology, I would like to focus on certain events that occurred during that time-period. Naturally, that will follow in a chronological order but I do want to focus on a number of specific issues and events during this period of time. I don't think there will be any dispute that the enclave itself fell on the 11th of July. My first question to you, sir, is: Did you see any superior officers from the corps or the Main Staff in or around Bratunac or your brigade command prior to the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw quite a few officers at the brigade command. Amongst them were members from the Drina Corps command and from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you provide their names, if you recall who you saw?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Main Staff, I saw General Mladic, Colonel Jankovic. And from the corps command, I saw General Krstic, General Zivanovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric, and I saw a lot of other officers, but those were mainly the officers from the corps command and from the Main Staff that I saw at the time, within the headquarters of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's focus on this Colonel Jankovic who you mentioned. Please tell the Trial Chamber when you recall him arriving and what he did, what was his activities upon his arrival? What did he tell you he was there for, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. Colonel Jankovic, as far as I can remember, arrived sometime on or around the 8th of July. He came to the Bratunac Brigade command headquarters. I don't know whether he reported at the time to my commander and whether they met. I can only assume, being a soldier, that that would be in line with military rules, for him to report to the commanding officer and then to proceed with the tasks that he was sent to perform. He came to my office, and he introduced himself as a colonel from the Main Staff and that he was from the intelligence department. Now, this is all I can tell you at this point, because prior to that moment, I had never seen Colonel Jankovic. Therefore I just accepted his words at face value, and I never checked what he said. He added that on orders from the Main Staff, he was sent down to help me, because I was a reserve captain, and the operation in question was huge and a complex one, and he said that, as of that day, when he arrived onwards, the tasks that I was in charge of prior to that, that is to say, liaison communication with international organisations including the Dutch battalion, he would take over, as well as all other intelligence operations relating to Srebrenica, and also, intelligence and security support. And he also said that we would be sitting together in the same office. So during that period, which started on the 8th, until, I don't know exactly where -- when he left, but he was among the last people who left the Bratunac Brigade, we selected a number of documents in those last few days, and he took those documents away with him. So he worked all the time with me in my office. He wrote his reports there and sent his reports from that office, and I remember that his reports had the heading of the Bratunac Brigade. Since I was sitting in the same office with him, I knew what he wrote in those reports because I sometimes personally went to the communications centre for those reports to be dispatched to the higher levels. So that's what I can tell you about Colonel Jankovic. We were working together throughout the whole period.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You described to us during the last couple of days of your testimony the process by which intelligence information would come to you; sometimes from the battalion, sometimes from other sources, and how you would report that information, both to your commander and up your intelligence and security line. Did you continue to engage in those activities while Colonel Jankovic was filing his reports, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I continued to do my regular work, and essentially nothing changed. I did not stop being the chief of the organ. I did not stop reporting to my commander. In other words, I continued to work as usual to carry out the tasks that I was authorised to carry out, and there were no problems in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during the course of your reporting, and during the course of Colonel Jankovic's reporting, were you aware as to whether you and he were sending reports to the same superior organs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I cannot tell you accurately about each and every document, whether it went both to the Drina Corps command and the Main Staff, but, in principle, our reports were identical because we worked from the same office, we harmonised our information, we exchanged information. The information that I received from the ground, I don't know how he obtained his information, though, but basically all the intelligence and all the reports were identical. They dealt with the same topics, they contained the same information, and the requests that we may have had, depending on what we put in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during the period of time of the actual attack on the enclave from the 6th of July through the 11th of July, and let's focus now on the time-period during which Colonel Jankovic was working from your office, were there also, do you recall, requests coming down to the brigade from your superior commands or professional organs for information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the translation is correct, but I believe I understood your question. Are you asking me whether there were any requests for information coming down to us from the superior commands?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My answer is affirmative. The corps command insisted and demanded that they be informed on a regular basis and also to receive extraordinary reports perhaps every half an hour, or every five minutes, if necessary, if new, important information arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during the VRS attack on the enclave, did you come to learn that the targets of the attack included, in addition to military targets, such as elements of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the targets also included civilians or civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me if I had ever seen a document or an order to that effect, that is to say, that civilians were the targets, I can tell you that I had never seen such a document, and I had never seen anything in writing confirming that the civilians were the object of the attack. If you're asking me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Actually, sir, I wasn't asking you that question. But since you've put your answer that way, let me just ask you: Would you ever expect to see, in a VRS order or communication, an explicit order to target civilians?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not expect that, of course. And no one in his right mind would write up any such thing, let alone a commander. In an order at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you see, in orders and documents, references to observing the Geneva Conventions in your experience?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understand the question, but the interpretation I'm receiving is mirrored in the way I'm answering the questions. Now, if you're asking me whether I understand this, whether I understand that there is an particular section of the Geneva Conventions that refers to the treatment of civilians, then that is a different question altogether. In every order, there is regulation of the status of civilians and things that have to do with prisoners and civilians. So that is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My specific question was, sir, was do you recall, in orders that you received, specific references to the Geneva Conventions and specific orders not to harm civilians, based on the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember such orders, and I think that one of the orders that I remember right now, as for the preparation of the order or the order itself of the Drina Corps for carrying out combat operations, something like that. I think that's the name. In that order it says, inter alia, that when carrying out combat operation, the principles enshrined in the Geneva Conventions should be abided by, and that is what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We'll leave that there for the moment, sir. Now, my original question was really getting at something else. Did you ever have -- did you receive any reports or information that civilian targets were attacked during the VRS operation against Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific in terms of period that you are referring to. I would appreciate that so that I would know exactly which period have you in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The period I have in mind would be the actual, during the course of the actual attack. Were civilian targets struck or aimed at; were civilians the targets of any of the VRS forces; and when did you learn this; and what was the source of the information? And I'm not referring to a written report -- when I say, Did you receive any reports or information, I'm not referring necessarily to an official written report, but did you become aware that civilians were targeted during the attack.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that during my previous testimony I spoke about that. I am not familiar with the plan of artillery fire and I don't know exactly which targets were engaged. However, what I know for sure is that during the attack on Srebrenica, inter alia, it was the town of Srebrenica itself that was a target. I think I said that during my previous testimony. For me that is a civilian target. The town itself, full of inhabitants, people, as it was. That was that kind of target as far as I'm concerned. If you are asking me now, I mean, if the question pertains to the period from the 11th, when the civilians were moving towards Potocari, then, again, I testified about that in the Popovic case. I know with full reliability, that is to say, that I received information to the effect that the target of fire from the positions of the 2nd Infantry Battalion from the B1 gun were civilians. Let me conclude by saying that civilians were targeted, a column of civilians, a huge column of civilians that was moving towards the Potocari base, or, rather the UNPROFOR base in Potocari, and they were moving from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what kind of weapon is a B1 gun, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A B1 gun is an artillery piece that was on the positions of my 2nd Infantry Battalion, roughly, that elevation, that peak, is called Zvijezda or Kokarda in that area. The B1 gun is the weapon that could target directly, that could involve direct fire. It was aimed at Potocari, the position of Potocari directly. Of course, it could target left and right as well. The road, also it could target everything within its range and everything that one could see. But Potocari, that position, was directly placed in such a way that it could be targeted directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn your attention for a few moments to the three meetings at the Hotel Fontana. The Trial Chamber has heard a lot of evidence about those meetings on the night of the 11th and the morning of the 12th, so I don't think we'll need to go through a detailed account of those three meetings. But let me just ask you a couple of questions about them. With respect to the first meeting at the Hotel Fontana, do you recall how you found out that there would be a meeting held there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that, that a meeting would be held at the Fontana hotel. That's what I found out from Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber briefly what your role was during this first meeting and where you were physically during it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. After Colonel Jankovic told me that this meeting would be held at the Fontana hotel that evening around 2000 hours, he said to me that I should make sure that a translator should be there. Of course, I called the military police commander. I asked him to send a policeman to find a translator called Petar Uscumlic. My task was to secure the Fontana hotel, that was the hotel where the meeting was supposed to be held. Namely, the hotel should be empty. It should be physically secure, and I should bring a translator to translate at the meeting. I was told that the -- that the meeting should be attended by the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, and that the meeting would be attended by the commander of the Dutch battalion, Colonel Karremans. Of course, after I provided for the translator, I went to Fontana. I agreed with the commander of the military police to involve the police and to be presently personally at the venue of the meeting. So the commander of the police, the police and I were the ones who provided security there at the actual venue where the meeting was supposed to be held. Before the meeting, well, I don't know exactly when Colonel Jankovic came to Fontana but in the first hall or room, I can draw that, I can explain what this Fontana looks like, so in this first room, we were waiting for their arrival. Jankovic, Petar Uscumlic and I were waiting for General Mladic to arrive with his team. General Mladic arrived just before 2000 hours in Fontana. We greeted him. Colonel Jankovic reported to him as to what was going on. We introduced Petar Uscumlic to him. Petar Uscumlic did not say his name, he just said his last name, Uscumlic. And it seemed to General Mladic that the interpreter was therefore a Muslim, and quite simply, he started shouting and he threw him out. So Colonel Jankovic and I remained in that room. The Dutch officers came, and in a small room, this first meeting was held. So my role was to provide for all of this, together with the commander of the military police. When the meeting started -- well, it was a small room. And the door is a sliding door that closes and opens. So it was open, and in that small room, the first meeting was held. I was three, four, or five metres away, maximum, to the left, in relation to the room where the meeting was being held, so I was in a place where I saw what was happening, where I heard what was being discussed, and basically, that would be it. That is what happened before the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And as I said, the Trial Chamber is -- has seen and heard a lot about that first meeting, so let's move from there. Did you return to your command following that first Fontana meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After that first meeting, General Mladic asked that a second meeting be held that evening, and, of course, that meeting was over. The Dutch went back. And I went to the command of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you returned to your command, do you recall receiving any information concerning the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information beforehand as well. Information was coming in intensively. It was already the evening, and there was quite a bit of information from the command, from the battalion commands, rather, but from the 2nd Infantry Battalion that was in immediate contact with Potocari from the observation post, from the positions of the 2nd Infantry Battalion there was constant reporting, to the effect that thousands of people were moving from Srebrenica towards Potocari, the UNPROFOR base there. That was the information that I received beforehand and during the course of the evening too. On the basis of everything I knew about the enclave beforehand and what the organs at the command knew as well, of the battalion commands, the 1st, 2nd and 3rd, but basically now I'm speaking about the information from the 2nd Battalion, we were making assessments to the effect that there were a lot of able-bodied men, military age among these persons. I have to explain something to the Trial Chamber. The fact that somebody is military age, able bodied does not mean in my view, now this is my assessment, my analysis, the fact that somebody is military age and able bodied does not mean that he is mobilised, engaged in a military way and is a member of a unit. So our assessment was that among the persons who were moving there who were on the move, who were civilians, there was between 1.500 to 2.000 military age, able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did you do with this information that you had beforehand and that was coming in and being gathered and that you were acquiring yourself? What did you do with that information, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the information I received on that day, in the afternoon and in the evening, just like on each and every previous day and following day, I communicated in writing to the command of the Drina Corps, that is to say, the department for intelligence and security affairs. As for this very same information, this was the practice that I observed, I provided that same information orally to the members of my brigade. That is to say, those to whom this information pertained. As for all of this information, I informed the commander about it later when we met up.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you referred to the commander and later when we met up, to whom are you referring specifically? And when you say "later," do you mean that day or some other day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't mean the 11th. I mean the following day, when we first met up after the operation. So that was the afternoon of the 12th. It is my commander, Blagojevic, whom I informed about all the information that had arrived. In the period while he was absent, I could not provide detailed information to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You told us about the second meeting at the Fontana hotel being scheduled. Again, we don't need to go through the details of that meeting. Please tell the Trial Chamber where you were physically during the second meeting at the Hotel Fontana?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that I explained in relation to the first meeting concerning my role, the role of the military police, and the commander of the military police, as for all my obligations with regard to the first meeting, they were the same with regard to the second meeting. The position of the meeting was the same, and I was there right in front of the meeting room where the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And immediately or upon the end of the meeting, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon the end of the meeting, General Mladic ordered that officers of the Dutch battalion and the representatives of the Muslim side be escorted to Potocari. After that, I carried out the order, got into the car, saw off the officers and the representative of the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And by this time, were you aware that there would be a third meeting the following morning?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber what you did starting in the morning of the 12th of July. And just take us, please, through the events of that morning.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I have to say that between the 12th and 13th of July, I was the duty operations officer. My assistant was Mirko Jankovic. And on that morning, as was the case with the previous meetings as well, my role had not changed at all. I knew what my duty was. I knew that the meeting was supposed to be held on the 12th at 10.00, and the military police, Mirko Jankovic as the commander, and I, as the chief of the intelligence and security organ in the brigade, took all measures for the hotel to be empty and secure and safe for the participants in the meeting. The meeting was scheduled for 10.00, and I knew exactly -- well, I didn't know the names, but I knew who was supposed to attend the meeting. On the basis of my information, the meeting was supposed to be attended by the representatives of the military authorities headed by General Mladic, the corps commander, and other officers who represented the Serb side. Then the meeting was supposed to be attended by the civilian authorities, or rather, the representatives of the civilian authorities, then the representatives of UNPROFOR and the representatives of the Muslim side. On the previous evening they were represented by Mandzic. That meeting was attended precisely by all of these people that I referred to, including the representatives of the Muslim side including a lady whose name I don't know. Nesib Mandzic and Nuhanovic were there, on their negotiating team. Since I attended the previous two meetings, I knew roughly what the content of this one would be. That is to say, that the overall situation was supposed to be discussed. It seems to me, on the basis of what I could infer, it was technical issues that were supposed to be discussed, how all of that would actually take place, including the forcible transfer of the Muslims from Potocari. So I did not attend that meeting. It started around 10.00. The representatives that I mentioned were there. They all arrived. What I wish to say what is important and what actually happened is, that before that meeting started, on that day, the 12th of July, in front of Fontana, I saw Mr. Popovic and Kosoric. These are two officers from the command of the Drina Corps, the chief of security and the chief of intelligence. We talked about the overall situation. Inter alia, we talked about what would happen further on with the people who had fled and who went to Potocari. Popovic told me that, quite simply, these people would be evacuated, that they would be transferred to Kladanj, that women and children would be transferred by buses, that that is the agreement that was reached. That they would be transferred to Muslim-controlled territory. And that military age men would be singled out and temporarily detained in the territory of the municipality of Bratunac. I asked him, Mr. Popovic, what about these people? What's going to happen to them? Why are we doing all of this? He said, sort of the way he spoke, he said that all the Balijas should be killed. I did not comment upon his statement. Quite simply, this conversation took five, six, or seven minutes, no longer than that. After that, or rather, during that conversation, we mentioned, or rather, I proposed, I said, all right these people will be singled out. They shall be detained. The most convenient facilities are those that are empty in Bratunac right now, and that was the elementary school of Vuk Karadzic, and then also the hangar, then the gym of that same school, Vuk Karadzic. And also there were some other facilities of the old secondary school from Bratunac. Djuro Pucar Stari was the name of that vocational secondary school. All of these facilities were within an area that could be secured with less troops. So, quite simply, they said yes, no problem whatsoever. So those were the facilities involved. Then in addition to that, my first impression or, rather, what I thought was that probably we will carry out this military triage, which is regular procedure. We'll get to Potocari, carry out that military triage. It was my understanding that we would single out or that those would be singled out who are reasonably suspected of having committed crimes, taking part in the killing of civilians, et cetera. We, and we information to that effect. However what happened was something that I did not expect. When the evacuation started, all of those who were men were singled out, regardless of their age, regardless of whether they were military conscripts, regardless of anything else. So what I saw was that all the men who were in Potocari were singled out. Then there's another question. After that, when he said that all the Balijas should be killed, then we discussed where it was that these Balijas should be killed. Two locations were mentioned. The mine of Sase, first of all, and the second one, the Ciglane, the brick-laying facility. I am duty-bound to say that no one was ever taken to the Sase Mine or was anybody ever executed at Sase or Ciglane. After this brief conversation, they went to this meeting. After the meeting, I met up, or, rather, Colonel Jankovic came out and said the following to me, that I should help. I have to explain this in the previous testimony, I used the word "coordination", literally not knowing what it means in military terms. But in my statement, I'm not going to say anything that is contrary to what I did. I'm just not going to use the word "coordination" because I really believe that that is not the appropriate term. Then Mr. Nikolic [sic] said to me, in the forthcoming period, you should help, have this operation carried out as it should be. He meant the operation of transferring civilians from Potocari to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there for a moment, sir. I notice number one in the transcript that there's a reference to Mr. Nikolic. This is at line -- page 20, line 7, what we have on the transcript is: "Then Mr. Nikolic said to me, in the forthcoming period, you should help, have this operation carried out." Who did you mean? I don't think you meant Mr. Nikolic. Who was telling you this? I think you had a slip of the tongue, sir.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it was my slip of the tongue. After the meeting, it was Mr. Jankovic who came out. Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And just so we have it clear in the record, when you refer to Colonel Jankovic, you're referring to the Main Staff colonel who occupied your office, starting on the 8th of July - is that correct? - as opposed to Mirko Jankovic who was the komandir of the military police platoon. Because we have two Jankovics.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now I just want to go back for a second to this conversation you had with Mr. Popovic prior to the third Fontana meeting. You told us that two locations were mentioned; two possible execution locations. Who proposed those two locations to Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I wouldn't even call it a proposal. To put it simply, we were discussing this subject. Mr. Popovic and Mr. Kosoric knew the Sase Mine, just as I did. I think that they first -- they were the first to mention the Sase Mine. After that, I spoke about it as well, and then we talked about those facilities together. I don't know who it was who mentioned it first. All three of us were discussing this particular location.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about the Ciglane brick-works. Do you remember who mentioned that location first?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know who mentioned it first. I know that we discussed those facilities. And one more thing. Later on, I found out, I don't know what the source of this information, but I received information that certain officers - I don't know which officers - went to see the area of the brick-works and the Sase before anything happened. I don't know who it was and when they went there. I heard that from the manager of the brick-works, who was saying that they used to come to the Ciglane brick-works. I think in this name is Nedjo Nikolic. Anyway, he was the manager of the brick-works at the time and he said that some officers used to come there even before the fall of Srebrenica. And he said that they discussed that. So I don't claim anything. I never verified this information. I'm not sure about it. But that's what I heard. Whether it is true or not, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during the third Fontana meeting, sir, where were you physically located? Were you in that same position just outside the room, or were you somewhere else for that third meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While this third meeting was going on, I wasn't in the room itself. The reason for that is that it was pretty crowded. Many people attended the meeting, and I simply thought that I, as the intelligence organ, cannot hear anything new there. They were discussing technical matters related to the number of the buses, the quantity of fuel, the escort and similar things. So I wasn't inside Fontana. I sat at the reception for a while, and that is a space that is separate from the space where the meeting was held. After that, I was in front of the hotel; I walked around. I was checking the police that was providing the security, and I wasn't inside, and I don't know the details about this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment. Just a follow-up question to this: On page 17, line 25, we see in the transcript that you said, and I would like to ask you to clarify that: "Since I attended the previous two meetings, I knew" - and I think there's a mistake - "... what the content of this one would be." And this refers to the third meeting. Where have you been during the first two meetings? Did you attend them, or were you present in the surrounding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I want to be precise. I attended the first two meetings in the Fontana hotel. And I was at a place from which I could see what was going on. However, I wasn't one of the participants in the meeting. I didn't represent anybody at the meeting and I didn't take part in the meeting in that sense. So, at the first meeting, the participants were General Mladic, General Jankovic and later General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... That is not my question. Sorry, this is not my question. I would like to know where precisely you have been during these meetings, in the room or outside the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, I wasn't inside that room. It's a small space. It's a small room and I was three, four, or five metres outside, in a bigger room, from which then you can enter the small room. Maybe I can draw a sketch. That would be the easiest way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I just wanted to know your position while the meeting was going on. Thank you very much. Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to go back to when Colonel Jankovic came out of the third Fontana meeting and gave you some instructions. Now, if I understand you correctly, you don't want to describe, in a military sense, some of your activities as coordination, to use that technical term. And if I understand you correctly, that's because you understand that word in a military sense to connote actual command authority. Is that -- do I have that correct? Do I understand your position correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you understood me well, yes. Yes, you understood me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, just so you know, the Prosecution's position is not that you were, in fact, a commander in the sense that, for example, Colonel Blagojevic was a commander. We understand that. What I want to focus on are your acts, what you actually did, and what you observed. Now, what did, if you can recall as precisely as possible, what did Colonel Jankovic tell you to do and what to expect?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember is that Colonel Jankovic told me that I should help to carry out this operation in Srebrenica. And as I've already stated, this operation also included the transfer of the women and children by buses to the territory controlled by the Muslims in Kladanj, while the able bodied, military aged Muslims should be temporarily separated and detained. There's a question that I posed to Colonel Jankovic. I asked who was going to do all this and what was going to take place in Potocari. He said the following: The activities relating to this operation had already been agreed. It means that the commanders which were to be engaged in Potocari had already received their assignments. He said that they are already in Potocari. Now, when it was, where they received those assignments, and from whom, that I wouldn't know. I only know what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in this conversation with Colonel Jankovic, was the execution of the Muslim men discussed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Colonel Jankovic did not mention this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did he give you the name of anyone, any officer in particular, to connect with in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He mentioned an officer, among other officers, called Dusko Jevic. He was an officer from the Special Police Brigade of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Jevic have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember it correctly, his nickname was Stalin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you did and what you saw in Potocari on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, as I already written in the statement, I spent part of the time in the operations room and part of the time in Potocari. In Potocari, I recognised, because I knew them, members of some units that were engaged in Potocari, people who were present in Potocari on the 12th. If it's necessary, I can list their names and the units that were present in Potocari. Now, as far as I know for sure, there were parts of the Bratunac police there. Then, parts of the 2nd Infantry Battalion. A little bit later, during the day, also the representatives of the 3rd Infantry Battalion arrived. Further on, there were members of the public security station in Bratunac. So members of the civilian police. Then, there were parts of the 10th Sabotage Detachment of the Main Staff. Also present were the members of the police from the 65th Protection Regiment of the Main Staff, from Nova Kasaba, they were headquartered in Nova Kasaba. Then, there were also parts of the military police from the Drina Corps command. And the soldiers from the detachment called the Drina Wolves, Vukovi Sa Drine. I'm not sure if I maybe forgot to mention somebody now, but these are people that I knew. A number of them had been engaged in Bratunac before. I mean here the police forces from the corps and from the 65th Protection Regiment. Later on I realized that what Colonel Jankovic had told me was true. The forces in charge of the evacuation were already there. My task was to help those people. By that I mean to help the officers and the units because I was a local inhabitant and I knew the situation and the area very well, and I also knew a large number of people who were there. What I helped on the 12th was mainly the help to Dusko Jevic. There was some problems, you know. First, there were problems with water. I think that Major Kingori asked me to secure some water, so I went to Bratunac and secured a cistern of water to be brought to Srebrenica. And then there was a huge crowd around the buses when the buses arrived and they had to turn. That's when I told Mr. Jevic that all this should be moved 2 or 300 metres away, to an area that was a bit wider. That's where the buses could have been parked and all this could have been performed more easily on that spot. Then, further on, what I was doing during all this was solving the problems that arose when the transport began. But I have to mention one more thing, what I saw before the transport itself began. When the separation began, in Potocari, General Mladic was present there and other people. I am not going to list them all. I think that there are few officers from the Main Staff and from the brigade commands who were not present in Potocari on the 12th. I can tell that you everybody was there present, and everybody wanted to see that. When the separation began, I know this for sure because I saw it, that there was General Mladic and Ljubisa Borovcanin and the commander of the specials, and Jevic, and other officers. And I saw something that was terrible. I saw mistreatment of those who were separated. I saw beating, cursing. I saw when they were separated. I saw that they were taking away their personal belongings, their bags, their money, everything that they had. And the people who were separated were then temporarily detained in some abandoned Muslim houses. Later on, they were transferred to Bratunac. So cursing, mistreating, beating, taking away of their property, throwing away of the personal belongings, that's what I saw when I was present there on the spot. In my testimony, I expressed my regret, that I did not react in this situation. I said then, and I'm saying this now, that it was my obligation, regardless of the consequences, and that I had to at least try to protect those people. In my testimony, I said that I did not do that and that I regret it. However, there is a fact that I would like to mention here, and that's through -- I simply didn't have the strength, didn't have the force, didn't have the units. I didn't have the authority as well, by this, I mean command authority with which I could prevent it. I could maybe go against it as a human being. I did a similar thing back in 1992 and I ended up in hospital. And to be quite honest, there was the 10th Sabotage Detachment there and the Drina Wolves and others and because of them, I simply couldn't do anything to protect those people, although I really disagreed with what was going on. I kept my silence. I didn't react. I didn't help. But, on the other hand, I didn't touch anybody and I didn't do anything. That's what I wanted to say. The transport began between 1.00, half past 1.00 or 2.00. I wouldn't know more precisely. As far as I know, and I testified about it, the first convoys contained a certain number of men. Why? I think I testified about it, and that no special comment is needed here. Those men were there for propaganda purposes. It wasn't something done in good faith. That's my personal opinion. It may be untrue, but that's my personal opinion. Later convoys that went to Kladanj were mostly empty. Excuse me, by that I meant to say that there were no men in them; only women and children. And I would just like to say one more thing. You asked me what else I did on the 12th. When the convoys started to leave, there were problems about the passage of the convoys through the town. Civilians gathered there. Mostly, they were mothers of the combatants who had been killed and their relatives. So the buses had to pass through the Bratunac town and during their passage through town, maybe 7 or 800 metres, the buses were stoned. I endeavoured to resolve the situation, to engage the civilian police, and to engage some people in the military police in order to prevent all this. And then when I wasn't in Potocari, I would return to the operations room. And then I would receive everything that would come in, and I would report about everything that I was requested to report on. While I was absent, I was replaced in the operations room by junior officers from the operations sector from the logistics, from the quartermaster service, and others. So when I returned, I had all the information they received from the superior command. So this in briefest possible terms how it went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I make a note. You said on page 28, lines 8 and 9, "I think I testified about it, and that no special comment is needed here." Just to remind you, but especially the Prosecution, this is a viva voce witness. The previous testimonies are not in evidence in this case. Just to clarify the situation. And another thing. You said on page 27, and I quote, line 1 through 4: "I think that there are few officers from the Main Staff and from the brigade commands who were not present at Potocari on the 12th. I can tell you that you everybody was there present and everybody wanted to see that." What do you mean by "everybody was there"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that on the 12th, the first day after the Srebrenica enclave officially fell and the Serb military police forces entered Potocari, all the officers who were present on that day in the zone of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade in Bratunac, also were in the enclave. By this, I mean to say that they were in Potocari and they saw everything that I saw going on in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, what do you mean by "all of them"? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I can list the names, if you want. First, my brigade and the officers of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm specifically interested in the Main Staff you was -- you were referring to that and in the Drina Corps command. Were all members of the Main Staff and all members of the Drina Corps command present in Potocari on the 12th, where you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe just one reservation: All those who were in Bratunac at the time, not all the members of the Drina Corps command. Those who were not there were not there, of course. So from the corps command, it was General Krstic, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric, Colonel Acamovic -- the chief of transport service, Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic. Then General Mladic. Colonel Jankovic. The commanders of the brigade that took over Srebrenica. The commander of combat groups that took over Srebrenica. Then the officers from the police. I listed those whom I could remember from the Main Staff, and those are the people who were in Potocari at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just need some clarifications, if you can give. At today's transcript, page 27, in answer to the previous question, you have said the following questions -- you have said the following: "I did a similar thing back in 1992 and I ended up in hospital." Can you please explain what you did and how you ended up in hospital? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. In 1992, at the very beginning of the war, sometime in May, conflict broke out in Bratunac. At the time, or before the -- the conflict, I was the assistant commander for intelligence affairs. When the conflict broke out, in the Bratunac staff, the commander was a Muslim, deputy commander was a Muslim, the logistics man a Muslim too. And just before the conflict broke out, they left for Tuzla. They were afraid of everything that took place after that in Bratunac. I remained in the staff, and since there was nobody else in the staff except me and one assistant for the call-up and one clerk for operations and training, I received a temporary assignment to lead the staff. It wasn't really a staff anymore. It had disintegrated. The Muslims left, the commander, the assistant commander and the assistant for the logistics, they left, and only three Serbs remained. And that's when I was performing that duty. On that fateful day, when I was attacked, they -- there were volunteers in Bratunac, as well as certain people from Bratunac itself, the village of Kravica. The neighbours were the Muslims in Sandici. And up to that point, the operations were going on related to the combat in Bratunac and taking over of certain territories. A group of the volunteers, together with the chief of the MUP, together with the group from the Kravica village, which is purely Serb village, and Sandici is purely Muslim village, they went by cars, without any approval, without any plan. They entered with their cars, passed through the check-point, and entered the village of Sandici. People in the village, Muslims, armed people opened fire and there were some people who were killed on that occasion. Among them, it -- among those people who were killed was the chief of the public security station, Milosevic, and I was blamed for everything that happened. So people from the village of Kravica blamed me, saying that I was responsible for it, saying that I didn't give them the military, that I didn't give them the reinforcements. When they asked me whether I would allow them to go and evacuate them, I said that I'm not going to ban anything but I'm certainly not going to order somebody to go and evacuate the people who went there of their own free will. That's when I was attacked and mistreated, and after that, I was sent to the hospital. I was in hospital in Serbia, in Sabac, and after that I was transferred to Belgrade for treatment. And then after that, I had to re-convalesce for about four or five months. Now how I looked like and what happened and what happened at the hospital, I can provide a full set of documents. I don't have it here, but I can provide it if the Trial Chamber is generally interested in knowing what happened at the time. I truthfully said that I couldn't stand to see children that I taught being killed in Bratunac. And all these things actually related to these killings that were committed by both the Serb and the Muslim side. As I said, all this is contained in documents. After I recovered from the shock, I told the doctor that I cannot any longer observe how the children from the school where I taught were being killed in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have another question, if I may. Just very briefly please, don't go into great detail. At page 28, lines 9 and 10, have you said -- maybe I should give it more context. "I think I testified about it and that no special comment is needed here. Those men were there for propaganda purposes." Which men are you referring to here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. That referred to the first convoy. Maybe I was not clear enough. So I was talking about the first convoy that left Potocari towards Kladanj. And there were Muslim refugees, women and children in that convoy. However, among them was a number of Muslim men who were fit for military service. So there were men, a number of men in this first convoy, and I said, given the fact that I saw a lot of things and -- before that and what I saw afterwards, when all the able-bodied men were separated, I assert here that that was just done as a means of propaganda, that they wanted to show to the international community that there were men among the people in convoy and that we were doing nothing wrong. That was my impression. However, later on, that turned out to be true, because there were no men in subsequent convoys other than in the first one. And if I may give you an additional confirmation of what I'm telling you now. I have information that a number of these people, of course, I cannot validate that because I have no proof - that a number of men from this first convoy en route at the check-point in Kravica, Konjevic Polje and Tisca, that is to say, just before they crossed over to the Muslim-controlled territory, a number of these men were separated at these check-points. This particularly refers to Tisca check-point, so at the very crossing where they disembarked from the buses, they were separated and detained. This is the information that I have. I don't know if it is true but I would like to tell you this. I don't want to keep quiet about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's really time for the first break. We must have the first break now and resume five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Thayer, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I -- I note that I'm arriving at the unsatisfactory situation about 20 minutes left of my eight-hour estimate. I can tell the Trial Chamber I've cut a number of exhibits from my examination. I've tried to limit and focus the examination but I will respectfully request some additional time to complete this examination as I think it needs to be completed. I'm trying to do not too much detail, but enough so that the important points are brought out for the Trial Chamber. I will have a couple of more documents when we're done with the narrative portion of Mr. Nikolic's testimony but I will need to exceed my eight-hour estimate, and I ask for the Court's indulgence and patience with that. I think we've hit a lot of important issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I need a specific request. How much additional time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I could have to the end of this session. I can do that without having to rush unnecessarily, without having to elide issues which the Trial Chamber may want to hear something about. So if I could have to the end of the session, I think we'll be able to really do the job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the same would be the case for the Defence during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to pick up with Potocari on the 12th and the 13th. You described a number of units being present on the 12th. You mentioned civilian police. And at one point, as it was translated, you mentioned Bratunac police. My question simply is: Were there elements of the Bratunac Brigade military police present in Potocari on the 12th and 13th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I answered this question. I think I did mention the military police unit. Elements of the Bratunac Brigade were engaged in Potocari on the 12th and 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you also mentioned the 65th Protection Regiment, and you indicated that their police unit was there. Again, is that a military police unit that's attached to the 65th Protection Regiment, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that that was the police attached to the 65th Regiment. As far as I know, but, again, don't take my word for it, because I'm not an expert in organisational structure of a regiment, but, as far as I know, they do have police forces as their elements. In any case, elements from the 65th Protection Regiment were engaged in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, just to clarify, this may be obvious to you, sir, but we're talking about a military police. We're not talking about civilian police when we're talking about the 65th Protection Regiment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We are talking about military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated before the break at one point that you reported to your commander, Colonel Blagojevic, about certain events. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what it was that you reported to him on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I informed Colonel Blagojevic about all the events that occurred on the 12th of July during the day and until the moment I reported it to him in the evening. So I informed him about all the issues that I already mentioned earlier, and I wouldn't like to repeat myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And without getting into details, did you report to him what your activities were on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told him that on the 12th, although he did know that anyway, that I was duty operations officer, first in Potocari, and that I was also engaged in the preparations for the meeting. I told him what I did and what the commander of the military police did with that respect. I also informed him about the situation in Potocari. I reported everything that I did and saw to him. But I think it is necessary for me to tell you that my commander, regardless of the fact that it was my duty to inform him about everything, my commander had that same information and a commander should have more information than anyone in the brigade. But, nevertheless, I informed him about the transportation issues, about the problems that I noticed, about the separation, about the intentions, and about everything that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And going into the 13th, Mr. Nikolic, did Commander Blagojevic adjust your tasks at all for the 13th of July? Did he tell you not to do anything, or did he tell to you do anything more, or different? Did he adjust them in any way?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no particular change, except that on the morning of the 13th, I finished my shift as a duty operations officer because the shifts started at 7.00 p.m. and lasted until 7.00 a.m. on the next day. As far as my tasks are concerned, with regard to the operation that took place on the 12th, was to continue with the activities that I was involved in on the previous day and that that was my main task, as far as I was concerned at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, in your experience when a superior officer does not interfere with the tasks or adjusts the tasks of a subordinate officer, what message does that communicate to the subordinate officer about whether or not to continue with the previous tasks?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, if there is nothing new, there are no objections, and there are no new orders, it is only logical for a person to continue what they were doing before, and that implies that, to my understanding, the commander agrees with what you are doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you go to Potocari on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I spent sometime at the brigade, and after that, I left for Potocari. And that was more or less my first task on the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you encounter Dusko Jevic, aka Stalin, again on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I saw him on the 13th, and I communicated with Dusko Jevic. That was the only officer, as far as I can tell, that I had direct contact with.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was there any information that you had acquired that you shared with Mr. Jevic on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the morning of the 13th, I already had a lot of information relating to the overall situation primarily to the movement of the Muslims and the capture of Muslims in the Konjevic Polje sector. When I saw Jevic on the 13th, I told him if he can get in touch with the police elements that were on the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road, to tell them that the people captured there should be gathered in Konjevic Polje and then transferred to Bratunac to the facilities that had already been designated for detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, what was your understanding of what would happen ultimately to those men who were captured along that road and transferred to the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of all the circumstances and everything I saw and heard beforehand, and in view of the overall situation that prevailed in this area, because I have to emphasise this, that the area where Srebrenica -- of Srebrenica, Bratunac is the area where a terrible crime and bloodbath took place in the previous period, and I knew everything that had happened before, because I was a native of that area, my conclusion was, and I was convinced that all those who were captured on that road would be taken to Bratunac and that they would end in the same way as those who were taken to Potocari. Because, in my opinion, there was no distinction between the treatment of those who were captured on the road and those who were separated on the 12th and detained in the Vuk Karadzic elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say "end up in the same way," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant just like all the others that were detained beforehand would be killed. Just as it happened with those who were taken to Bratunac. They were all killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to be clear on the record, I see at line 3 of page 39, what's written here, sir, is: "They would end in the same way as those who were taken to Potocari." Is that what you meant to say, that they would end up in the same way as the men taken to Potocari, or did you mean something else?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said those who were taken from Potocari and detained in the Vuk Karadzic elementary school in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now to move things along a little bit, on the 13th, it's fair to say you went to Konjevic Polje twice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Tell us about the first time you went there.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I went to Konjevic Polje was around 1230 hours, if I remember correctly, and the reason was, the information that along this road Bratunac-Konjevic Polje-Nova Kasaba, the commander of the Main Staff was to pass along that road. I took all the necessary security measures along the route of the corps commander or the commander of the Main Staff, and my duty was to check the situation on the road. Along with a member of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade, I travelled in a Golf car and I inspected that section of the road. Perhaps half an hour later, because the distance is about 20 kilometres, I arrived in Konjevic Polje. If you are interested in what I was doing in Konjevic Polje and the rest of it, I can tell you about that, but basically that was my first visit. If you want to hear about my next visit, I stayed in Konjevic Polje for a certain period of time, and then after General Mladic passed through, I returned to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you actually have personal contact with General Mladic in Konjevic Polje on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As he was passing through, he stopped in Konjevic Polje, and I reported to him in Konjevic Polje. I walked up to him. I greeted him, and I said, Commander, sir, all is well, the road is accessible, as one does report in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did General Mladic say anything to any of the prisoners who were present in that area?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were prisoners there already. And General Mladic actually addressed them, and said in the briefest possible terms that everything would be all right, that they would be transferred, that they should not worry, and that is what he said to them directly. After that, he set out towards his vehicles and behind him was his security detail, including the security detail from my Bratunac Brigade that escorted him all day. Already on the 13th, there were quite a few refugees and the situation was rather chaotic. I asked him, General, sir, what is going to happen to these people? What do we do with these people? And he did not say anything. He did not communicate verbally with me, he just did this with his hand. It was just a gesture, and it was clear to me what it was, this gesticulation of his. After that, he got into the car and went towards Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just so we can have a description on the record, sir, the motion you're describing General Mladic made with his hand was a flat wave with his palm down across his chest level from left to right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically the way I showed you. I can demonstrate it again, that's what you saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, that's fine. Sir we just need something in the transcript, something to memorialise it. And at some point did you also encounter a man by the name of Resid Sinanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, please, briefly tell us what that was about.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After, or rather, before I returned to Bratunac, in Konjevic Polje as far as the police was concerned - not the military, the civilian police - I was told by them that they had an important prisoner and they told me who it was. When they told me the name, it was Sinanovic, Resid Sinanovic. He is a man I knew all my life in Bratunac. He is a person who lived and worked in Bratunac all his life. In addition to the other duties he had, he was chief of police, chief of civilian police in Bratunac. Together with that policeman who went with me we got into the car. We took Resid. He sat in the back seat, and we brought him by car to the Bratunac Brigade. I personally and that policeman handed over Resid Sinanovic to the military police and we handed him over to directly to Zlatan Celanovic who worked there as a legal officer and basically conducted interrogations in 95 per cent of all cases. He interrogated prisoners of war and he did everything else that was related to the collection of information, questioning of prisoners of war, seeing whether there were elements of crime involved and so on. To the best of my knowledge Sinanovic was questioned by Zlatan Celanovic. There is a paper which is a record that he kept. While he was in Bratunac, he was visited by his friends, his Serb friends who lived and worked with him, and after that questioning, Zlatan Celanovic told me later that to the best of his knowledge and on the basis of the questioning, he was no criminal, there were no elements of crime involved at all, and that he decided to transfer him to the Vuk Karadzic school where the other prisoners were. As for my further knowledge, it is as follows. On the 14th, together with the convoy that went to Zvornik, that is to say, together with the other prisoners, Resid Sinanovic was transferred as well. You know just like I do what happened in the Zvornik brigade. Mass killings took place. Inter alia, according to the information gathered and the knowledge of my own lawyers, Sinanovic was wounded in Zvornik. He swam across the Drina. Zvornik is on the Drina river. He swam across the Drina river, and he found himself in another state, in the Republic of Serbia. He came to a tavern, the people who kept that tavern recognised him and took him to Banja Koviljaca. My lawyers, after I decided to admit my guilt and after my lawyers investigated all of that, as for the complete documentation regarding Sinanovic's stay in the hospital, they handed it over to the OTP. After that, my lawyers also informed me that they had established that Resid Sinanovic was taken over, that the police from Zvornik, I don't know which one, took him over and that as for this information that Resid Sinanovic was in the hospital, was provided by a lady doctor who had worked in Bratunac before that, and who used to be a neighbour. She and Resid Sinanovic lived on the same floor. She recognised him. She called the police in Bratunac, and they probably called the police in Zvornik, and according to the investigation of my lawyers, they came to realise that Resid Sinanovic was taken over from the hospital and liquidated, killed on the bridge between the Republic of Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to Mr. Sinanovic being treated in a hospital, was that hospital in Serbia or in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospital was in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber about your second trip to Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. My second trip to Konjevic Polje took place right after my return, after I was there the first time with the Golf car. The second time I went there was with the commander of the military police, Mirko Jankovic and the deputy commander, Mirko -- no, not Mirko, Milo Petrovic, sorry. We went in an APC. Mirko Jankovic, the commander of the military police, knew how to drive an APC. We took an APC that was at the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade and belonged to the Dutch battalion. It wasn't only one of them. Mirko Jankovic knew how to drive it. We took the APC and got into the APC and went in that direction. As we were moving in that direction, that was on the 13th, sometime in the afternoon, as far as I could see from Sandici all the way to Konjevic Polje, there were police forces of Republika Srpska, and along that road there were prisoners that were moving along in groups. In Sandici, there were some who had been taken prisoner there and then all the way up to Konjevic Polje. When I arrived in Konjevic Polje, there were already a great many prisoners there. I don't know what else you're interested in, in relation to that road or journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, do you recall there being a loud-speaker on the APC?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did anybody use that loud-speaker for any purpose?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mirko Jankovic, after we had passed Kravica, roughly after Sandici, used that loud-speaker that was in the APC, in addition to all the other equipment, Mile Petrovic was calling upon the Muslims to surrender. He used that loud-speaker for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on this trip, did any Muslim men, in fact, surrender to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As we were moving towards Konjevic Polje, at some point after Sandici, Pervani or I don't know exactly, but along that road, we caught up with a group of six Muslim men who were walking. We stopped the APC and we got the six Muslims into the APC and then we brought them to Konjevic Polje. We stopped the APC in Konjevic Polje in an area that was in front of the intersection and I said to Mirko, or rather, to Mile Petrovic that the prisoners should be taken to where the others were. After a while, Mile Petrovic returned. I was sitting right there by the intersection. On the left-hand side, there is a house when you're coming from Bratunac. It had been torched but there was a concrete terrace down there, a sort of porch, and there was a fire and they were preparing some food. I was sitting there. After a while, I heard a burst of gun-fire. Mile Petrovic walked up to me, and he says literally, Boss, I have just avenged my brother. And I said, You did what? And he said, I killed them. I asked him, What have you done? And he said there was a yellow cooperative building right there and then there is this small river, and he said that he took these people behind this yellow building and killed them. I didn't go there to see whether he had actually killed them or not. Quite simply, I was sick of everything. I didn't do anything about it. As I've said a countless number of times so far, I didn't do anything about it, and I should have done something about it. I should have reported it to Celanovic. I said to Celanovic what happened, but I didn't do anything official. I did not take any official measures and I think I was supposed to have done so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my apology, Mr. Prosecutor. Before we move on to another topic, I would like to go back to the transcript, page 40, but also page 41. Witness, on page 40, line 22 to line 24, you said that General Mladic said to the prisoners that nothing untoward would happen to them. And then, on page 41, line 5 to 8, when you asked General Mladic what would happen to the prisoners, he made a gesture that you also made in the courtroom. What does this gesture mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I know General Mladic, It is easy for me to know what he meant, but, believe me, in that area of mine where I live, in my country, that gesture and that reaction to my question, General, sir, what's going to happen to these prisoners actually? Well, what I can say to you is that I put that question with good reason, because I saw what was happening. I saw what was happening in Potocari. I saw the same promises in Potocari. And the distribution of chocolates and everything else, and I knew what was behind all of that. I knew what was in the making for these people. Also, when he did that with his hand, when I asked him, General sir, what will actually happen to these people because I did not believe, I personally did not believe what he was saying. And I asked him what's going to happen to these people and he did this with his hand. And, for me, that meant that these people would be killed. I could not draw any different conclusion from that reaction of General Mladic's. Indeed, afterwards, that is what happened to these people. They were detained, they were transferred to Bratunac and Zvornik and they were killed. Nothing else. Since I saw everything in Potocari, I could not draw any other conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
